s: A 52-year-old woman undergoes left mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection for invasive breast carcinoma. At her 2-week follow-up visit, the medial border of her left scapula lifts away from the chest wall when she pushes against a wall with both hands.
l: Injury to which nerve best explains this finding?
e: The **long thoracic nerve** (C5 to C7) runs down the medial wall of the axilla on the surface of serratus anterior, squarely in the field of axillary node dissection. Serratus anterior holds the scapula against the ribs, so its paralysis lets the medial border lift off when the patient pushes forward: a winged scapula. The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi and causes weak adduction and extension without winging, and the intercostobrachial nerve is purely sensory.

w.Thoracodorsal nerve: This nerve runs along the posterior axillary wall to latissimus dorsi; injury weakens adduction, extension and internal rotation of the arm, but the scapula stays flat.
w.Intercostobrachial nerve: The lateral cutaneous branch of T2 crosses the axilla carrying only sensation, so cutting it numbs the medial upper arm without any muscle weakness.
w.Medial pectoral nerve: It supplies pectoralis minor and the lower part of pectoralis major; damage weakens or wastes those muscles but does not release the scapula from the ribs.
w.Axillary nerve: It wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus to deltoid and teres minor; injury follows shoulder dislocation or fracture and weakens abduction instead.

et: Skin of the medial upper arm
Around the surgical neck of the humerus
bl: Winged scapula after axillary dissection means the long thoracic nerve to serratus anterior was injured.

pt.say: The first nerve card shows the long thoracic nerve on serratus anterior, whose injury gives a winged scapula.

s: A 58-year-old woman notices a change in her right breast. Examination shows a 2-cm hard, irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant. When she raises both arms above her head, the skin directly over the mass puckers inward.
l: Tumor involvement of which structure most directly causes the skin change?
e: Fibrous **Cooper ligaments** run from the dermis through the breast to the deep fascia. A carcinoma that infiltrates them provokes fibrosis that shortens the bands, so the skin they anchor is pulled inward, most visibly when raising the arms stretches the breast. Blocked dermal lymphatic vessels cause edematous peau d'orange skin instead, involved lactiferous ducts retract the nipple, and pectoral fascia invasion fixes the mass to the chest wall without dimpling.

w.Dermal lymphatic vessels: Tumor emboli in dermal lymphatics cause lymphedema of the skin, whose hair follicles stay tethered and give a pitted peau d'orange surface, typical of inflammatory carcinoma.
w.Lactiferous ducts: When tumor shortens the ducts that converge beneath the areola, the nipple itself is drawn inward; skin over a peripheral lesion is spared.
w.Pectoral fascia: Invasion through the retromammary plane into the deep fascia anchors the lesion so it moves with the contracting muscle; it does not pucker the skin.
w.Axillary lymph nodes: Nodal metastases produce a firm or matted lump in the armpit and stage the disease, but they cannot pull on skin over the primary tumor.

bl: Skin dimpling over a breast cancer means tumor has shortened the Cooper (suspensory) ligaments.

pt.say: The Cooper (suspensory) ligament runs from the skin to the fascia; the note at the bottom shows that shortening it pulls the skin inward.

s: A 61-year-old woman has a 4-cm mass in the lower inner quadrant of her left breast. With her arms relaxed at her sides, the mass can be moved slightly over the chest wall. When she presses her hands firmly against her hips, the mass no longer moves independently and shifts with the underlying muscle. The overlying skin is smooth.
l: Tumor extension into which structure explains this finding?
e: The breast normally glides over pectoralis major because the loose retromammary space separates it from the **pectoral fascia**. A carcinoma that grows across that space and attaches to the fascia becomes fixed: tensing the muscle by pressing on the hips makes the mass move with it. Fixation signals deep invasion. Cooper ligament involvement would dimple the smooth skin, and lactiferous duct involvement would retract the nipple.

w.Suspensory (Cooper) ligaments: Shortened suspensory bands pull the overlying skin into a dimple, and her skin is smooth; tethering to skin does not bind the lesion to muscle.
w.Lactiferous ducts: Tumor along the large subareolar ducts retracts or inverts the nipple; a peripheral lesion anchored to muscle points to a deeper plane.
w.Dermal lymphatic vessels: Dermal lymphatic emboli thicken and redden the skin into peau d'orange, a superficial change that leaves the deep gliding plane intact.
w.Internal mammary lymph nodes: These parasternal nodes receive lymph from medial tumors, but metastasis to them is not palpable and does not change how the primary lesion slides.

bl: A mass that moves with contracting pectoralis has invaded the pectoral fascia across the retromammary space.

pt.say: Tumor that crosses the retromammary space reaches the pectoral fascia, so the mass is anchored; the bottom note calls this fixation.

s: A 47-year-old woman is found to have a 1.8-cm invasive carcinoma in the upper inner quadrant of her right breast, 2 cm from the edge of the sternum. Before surgery, radiotracer is injected around the tumor. Lymphoscintigraphy shows the tracer flowing medially, away from the axilla, to a single node deep to the second intercostal space; no axillary uptake is seen.
l: Which lymph node group received the tracer?
e: About 75 percent of breast lymph drains to the axilla, but the medial quadrants also drain along the internal thoracic vessels to the **internal mammary** (parasternal) nodes, which lie deep to the intercostal spaces beside the sternum. A medial tumor can therefore send its sentinel node there. Level I and level III axillary nodes lie lateral and medial to pectoralis minor within the axilla, and supraclavicular nodes sit above the clavicle.

w.Level I axillary nodes: Level I nodes lie lateral to pectoralis minor in the lower armpit and receive most lateral-quadrant lymph; the scan showed no uptake there at all.
w.Level III (apical) axillary nodes: Apical nodes sit medial to pectoralis minor beneath the clavicle and are reached after levels I and II, so they are rarely the first stop.
w.Supraclavicular nodes: Nodes above the clavicle receive lymph after the axillary or parasternal chains; involvement marks advanced regional disease rather than a first stop.
w.Interpectoral (Rotter) nodes: These nodes lie between pectoralis major and minor and drain into level II; they belong to the axillary pathway, not the parasternal one.

et: Beside the sternum, deep to intercostal spaces
Can be first for medial tumors
Medial to pectoralis minor, under the clavicle
bl: Medial-quadrant tumors can drain first to the internal mammary (parasternal) nodes along the internal thoracic vessels.

pt.say: At the top left, the internal mammary nodes drain the medial quadrants along the internal thoracic vessels beside the sternum.

s: A 55-year-old woman has a 1.5-cm invasive ductal carcinoma in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast and no palpable axillary nodes. Before lumpectomy, blue dye and radiotracer are injected near the areola. The surgeon removes the first blue, radioactive node in the lower axilla, and frozen section shows no tumor.
l: Which conclusion is best supported by this result?
o: Further axillary dissection can be omitted
Level III nodes must be sampled next
The internal mammary chain must be dissected
The tumor is confined by its basement membrane
e: Lymph from a tumor reaches the axillary nodes in order, so the first node on the path, the sentinel node, predicts the status of the rest. A tumor-free sentinel node means the remaining axillary nodes are very unlikely to hold metastases, so **further axillary dissection can be omitted**, sparing the nerves and lymphatics at risk. Level III nodes are reached only after lower levels, and a negative node says nothing certain about blood-borne distant metastasis.

w.Level III nodes must be sampled next: Apical nodes lie beyond levels I and II on the drainage path; with a clean first node, isolated spread to them is uncommon, so routine sampling is unnecessary.
w.The internal mammary chain must be disse: Parasternal nodes matter mainly for medial tumors, and even then they are imaged or irradiated rather than routinely dissected; this tumor is lateral.
w.Distant metastasis has been excluded: Carcinoma also spreads through blood to bone, liver, lung and brain, so a clean node lowers the likelihood of metastasis but cannot rule it out.
w.The tumor is confined by its basement me: An invasive ductal carcinoma has by definition already crossed its basement membrane; node status reflects lymphatic spread, not whether invasion occurred.

et: Further axillary dissection can be omitted
Level III nodes must be sampled next
Spread through levels I and II first
The internal mammary chain must be dissected
Imaging of bone, liver, lung and brain
The tumor is confined by its basement membrane
bl: A tumor-free sentinel node predicts clean remaining nodes, so further axillary dissection can be omitted.

pt.say: The sentinel node, ringed at level I, is the first axillary stop; when it is clean, further axillary dissection can be skipped.

s: A 49-year-old woman who swims competitively had a right modified radical mastectomy with axillary node dissection 3 months ago. She now struggles to pull herself out of the pool and to reach into her back pocket with her right hand. Her scapula stays flat against the chest wall when she pushes against a wall, and light touch over the medial upper arm is normal.
l: Which nerve was most likely injured during the operation?
e: Pulling the body up and reaching into a back pocket need extension, adduction and internal rotation of the arm, the actions of latissimus dorsi. Its nerve, the **thoracodorsal nerve**, runs along the posterior axillary wall with the thoracodorsal vessels, close to the nodes removed in dissection. A long thoracic injury would wing the scapula, which is absent, and an intercostobrachial injury would numb the medial arm, which has normal sensation.

w.Long thoracic nerve: Loss of serratus anterior lets the medial scapular border lift away from the ribs; her flat scapula during a wall push rules this out.
w.Intercostobrachial nerve: Cutting this sensory T2 branch numbs the armpit and inner arm without weakness, yet her sensation there is normal and her deficit is motor.
w.Lateral pectoral nerve: It supplies the upper pectoralis major, which flexes and adducts the arm across the chest; injury weakens pushing and hugging, not pulling down and back.
w.Axillary nerve: Deltoid and teres minor lose power after humeral neck fracture or shoulder dislocation, weakening abduction; node surgery rarely reaches this nerve.

et: Flexion and adduction across the chest
Abduction beyond the first few degrees
bl: Weak extension and adduction with a flat scapula after axillary surgery means thoracodorsal nerve injury to latissimus dorsi.

pt.say: The middle card shows the thoracodorsal nerve to latissimus dorsi, whose injury weakens adduction and extension, her exact deficit.

s: A 30-year-old woman who is exclusively breastfeeding her 6-week-old son notices that milk begins to spray from both nipples whenever she hears him cry, even before he latches.
l: Contraction of which cells ejects the milk?
e: The cry triggers a conditioned reflex: the hypothalamus signals the posterior pituitary to release oxytocin, which binds receptors on the **myoepithelial cells** that wrap every alveolus and duct. Their contraction squeezes milk into the ducts and out of the nipple, the let-down reflex. Luminal epithelial cells synthesize milk under prolactin but cannot contract, and lactotrophs secrete prolactin rather than ejecting milk.

w.Luminal epithelial cells: The inner layer makes milk proteins and fat under prolactin and releases them into the lumen, but it has no contractile filaments to push milk out.
w.Areolar smooth muscle cells: Smooth muscle in the areola and nipple contracts to erect the nipple for latching; it does not surround the alveoli where milk is stored.
w.Intralobular stromal cells: The loose stroma around lobules is hormone-responsive and swells in the luteal phase, but it holds no contractile cells that expel milk.
w.Anterior pituitary lactotrophs: Lactotrophs secrete prolactin, which sustains milk synthesis between feeds; ejection depends on oxytocin from the posterior pituitary instead.

et: Outer layer of alveoli and ducts
bl: Oxytocin makes the myoepithelial cells around alveoli contract, producing milk let-down.

s: A 54-year-old woman has a 1.2-cm spiculated density on screening mammography. Core biopsy shows irregular nests and small glands of atypical epithelial cells scattered through a dense fibrous stroma. Immunostains for p63 and smooth muscle myosin heavy chain are positive in a continuous rim around adjacent normal ducts but are absent around the atypical nests and glands.
l: What does the absent staining around the atypical glands indicate?
o: Loss of the myoepithelial layer from invasion
e: p63 and smooth muscle myosin heavy chain mark **myoepithelial cells**, which normally form a continuous outer layer around ducts and lobules and persist around carcinoma in situ. Tumor cells that have broken through the basement membrane into the stroma form nests with no myoepithelial rim, so absent staining means invasive carcinoma, fitting the spiculated, desmoplastic mass. Sclerosing adenosis also looks infiltrative, but its compressed acini keep their myoepithelial layer and stain.

w.Sclerosing adenosis with compressed acin: This benign mimic distorts crowded acini with fibrosis, yet every acinus keeps a continuous p63-positive rim, which is exactly what these nests lack.
w.Lobular rather than ductal differentiati: Lobular carcinoma is identified by loss of E-cadherin, not by myoepithelial stains; both ductal and lobular in situ lesions keep a myoepithelial rim.
w.Overexpression of the HER2 receptor: HER2 status is read with a separate membrane immunostain or a gene amplification test; p63 and myosin say nothing about growth-factor receptors.
w.Lactational change in the lobules: Lactating lobules show dilated alveoli with vacuolated cells and milk, and their contractile outer layer is preserved to eject that milk.

et: Loss of the myoepithelial layer from invasion
p63 and smooth muscle myosin negative
p63 and smooth muscle myosin positive
Present in the in situ phase
bl: Absent myoepithelial staining (p63, smooth muscle myosin) around tumor nests means the carcinoma is invasive.

s: A pathology resident reviews breast tissue from a 28-year-old woman who died in a car crash 8 weeks after delivering a healthy infant. The lobules are enlarged and packed with dilated alveoli lined by cuboidal cells with vacuolated cytoplasm. Electron microscopy shows lipid droplets bulging from the apical surface and pinching off wrapped in a thin layer of plasma membrane and cytoplasm.
l: Which secretory mechanism releases the milk component described?
e: Milk fat is released by **apocrine secretion**: the lipid droplet pushes against the apical membrane and pinches off with a thin rim of membrane and cytoplasm, which becomes the milk fat globule membrane. Milk proteins such as casein leave the same cells by merocrine secretion, the exocytosis of secretory vesicles with no loss of cytoplasm. Holocrine secretion, in which the whole cell disintegrates, describes sebaceous glands.

w.Merocrine secretion: Exocytosis of vesicles releases milk proteins such as casein, and lactose, without losing any cell membrane, so it cannot explain membrane-wrapped fat droplets.
w.Holocrine secretion: Sebaceous glands release their product when the entire cell breaks down and is shed; lactating alveolar cells survive and keep secreting.
w.Transcytosis: Vesicles carry secretory IgA across the alveolar cell after binding the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor; this moves antibody, not the fat droplets described.
w.Paracellular diffusion: Leak between cells through loosened tight junctions lets sodium and plasma proteins into milk during mastitis; it does not package lipid in membrane.

et: How the product leaves the cell
Apex pinches off around the droplet
bl: Milk fat leaves alveolar cells by apocrine secretion; milk proteins leave by merocrine exocytosis.

s: A 29-year-old woman at 36 weeks' gestation asks why her breasts, which have enlarged greatly during pregnancy, are not yet producing milk, even though her serum prolactin is many times the nonpregnant level. Two days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and expulsion of the placenta, her breasts become firm and full, and copious milk production begins.
l: The onset of copious milk production after delivery is best explained by a fall in which hormone?
e: During pregnancy, estrogen, **progesterone** and prolactin build the lobules and alveoli, but the very high placental progesterone blocks prolactin's ability to switch on full milk synthesis. Expelling the placenta removes that source, and the fall in progesterone over the next few days releases the brake, so copious secretion begins while prolactin stays high. A fall in prolactin would reduce milk, and oxytocin controls ejection rather than production.

w.Prolactin: Prolactin remains high after delivery and rises further with each feeding; it is the hormone that drives milk synthesis, so its fall would stop lactation instead.
w.Oxytocin: Oxytocin surges during labor and suckling to contract myoepithelial cells and eject milk; it moves milk already made rather than starting synthesis.
w.Dopamine: Hypothalamic dopamine inhibits lactotrophs, so less dopamine would raise prolactin; but prolactin was already high before delivery without copious milk.
w.Human placental lactogen: This placental hormone falls after delivery too, but its main roles are maternal insulin resistance and mammary growth; its loss does not unlock secretion.

et: Builds alveoli; blocks full milk synthesis
bl: Placental delivery drops progesterone, releasing its block on prolactin, so copious milk production begins.
